At low laser power, the powder-coated absorptivity was reported to be about twice that of the bare polished discs. For bare materials, absorptivity changed slightly with increasing power until recoil-pressure-induced surface depression began; the resulting keyhole morphology increased absorption. Above the keyhole transition, absorptivity reached a saturation value for both bare and powder-coated samples. contexts.question: Context: we are writing our own physics-based (first-principles, no parameters fitted to keyhole data) model of laser keyholing and keyhole-mode melt-pool size for laser powder bed fusion of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend, to replace the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module where conduction models (Eagar-Tsai) fail. Settings: 1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam with 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s, 30-150 C plate. The model has three parts: (1) absorptivity from the Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid metal with multiple reflections ray-traced inside the keyhole; (2) the keyhole's depth and shape from an energy balance at a wall held near the boiling point (moving line/point sources, Kaplan-style local conduction, evaporation losses, recoil pressure against surface tension); (3) the melt pool as the liquidus isotherm of the resulting sources. We will check it against Gan et al. 2021 (Nat. Commun. 12, 2379) X-ray keyhole depths for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061 and SS316, and against the AM Module's maps. Question: what direct measurements of laser absorptance during spot or line melting relate the absorbed fraction to the depression or keyhole depth, width or aspect ratio, for aluminium alloys (Al6061, AlSi10Mg, pure Al) and for comparison Ti-6Al-4V, 316L and IN625? Include integrating-sphere measurements made together with X-ray imaging (e.g. Simonds et al. 2021, Applied Materials Today), calorimetry (Trapp et al. 2017; Ye et al. 2019), and any keyhole-mode absorptance for Al at 1 um. Give the numbers: power, speed or dwell, spot size, measured absorptance, depression depth and width, and the reported relation (for example absorptance against depth/width), with DOIs, so that a ray-tracing absorptivity model can be checked against them. Also: what flat-surface absorptance at 1.06-1.07 um has been measured for liquid aluminium, and does a Drude model reproduce it?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the integrating-sphere method used to calculate time-resolved absorptance, but it does not provide the AM-Bench 2022 experimental conditions or measured bare-aluminum results requested. In the described method, absorptance is calculated as A(t) = PA(t)/Po(t), where absorbed power is obtained from the difference between input and reflected power: PA(t) = Po(t) − PR(t). The input-power waveform is measured using a diffusely reflecting target and scaled to the measured laser energy. Reflected power is derived from the photodiode signal using PR(t) = C·SR(t)·10^ND, with calibration factor C determined from a known-reflectance Infragold target having r = 0.933 at 1070 nm. The excerpt mentions laser powers and pulse-measurement procedures, including calibration measurements at approximately 50.5–67.3 W, but these are not identified as AM-Bench 2022 bare-aluminum conditions, nor are scan speed, spot size, X-ray-imaging results, or aluminum absorptance values reported. Consequently, the requested integrating-sphere and Advanced Photon Source measurements cannot be recovered from this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the AM-Bench 2022 asynchronous experiments on bare solid aluminum (Al 5182), using samples cut from NIST Standard Reference Material 1241c. The experiments were performed at the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratory and included both stationary and scanned laser exposures. The aluminum specimens were 1 mm thick, wire-EDM cut, and polished to a mirror-like finish. Integrating sphere radiometry measured absolute laser power absorption (absorptance), while high-speed X-ray imaging recorded projected melt-pool behavior simultaneously. X-ray images were acquired at 50,000 frames per second with 2.5 µs exposure times, and absorptance measurements had 40 ns time resolution. The laser diameter at the sample surface was 122.5 µm (1/e²), and the sample surface was tilted 7° to capture specular reflection. Although the challenge supplied laser power, scan speed, laser spot size, and material composition, the excerpt does not state the numerical laser power, scan-speed values, or measured aluminum absorptance values. contexts.context: The excerpt describes two AM-Bench 2022 bare-aluminum experiments. For the stationary-laser tests, the integrating sphere measured absorptance with 40 ns temporal resolution during a 1.982 ms exposure. The delivered laser power was 501 W, and the laser spot diameter at the sample surface was 122.5 µm (1/e²). The sample surface was tilted by 7° so the integrating sphere could capture specularly reflected light. X-ray imaging was used concurrently to observe melt-pool/keyhole evolution. Keyhole formation in the stationary experiment was defined at relative absorptance of at least 35%, occurring at approximately 0.189 ms. For the scanned-line experiments, the laser power was 473 W, exposure duration was 1.980 ms, and scan speed was 700 mm/s. The scanned-beam keyhole criterion was relative absorptance of at least 25%. The excerpt states that the scanned absorptance data exhibited oscillations, which none of the simulations reproduced, and that simulations generally underestimated pre-keyhole average absorptance while agreeing better after keyhole formation. It does not provide the full numerical measured absorptance averages or the Advanced Photon Source facility details; those values appear to be contained in the referenced figures or other portions of the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide numerical emissivity, reflectivity, refractive index n, extinction coefficient k, or normal-incidence absorptance for liquid aluminum at 1064 nm (approximately 1 µm), nor does it report levitation measurements of aluminum. It gives general modeling context: the Drude model describes metals using free-electron behavior and can qualitatively explain optical properties, particularly at longer infrared wavelengths. However, it omits resonant interband absorption and therefore may fail at shorter wavelengths, including the near-infrared and visible ranges. A Drude–Lorentz model adds interband Lorentz oscillators to improve the description, although the excerpt notes that temperature-dependent oscillator parameters were not known and initially only the electron density was varied with temperature. The article also emphasizes that roughness strongly affects ellipsometric measurements, so smooth surfaces are important. These statements may help assess whether a simple Drude model should reproduce liquid-aluminum data at 1064 nm, but the excerpt contains no aluminum-specific measurements or numerical optical constants from which emissivity, reflectivity, or absorptance can be calculated.

contexts.context: The excerpt states that Gan et al. measured keyhole evolution using ultrahigh-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging, with keyhole depth quantified directly from in situ images. The keyhole aspect ratio is defined as e* = e/r0, where e is keyhole depth and r0 is laser spot radius. However, the provided pages do not report the material-specific numerical keyhole depths, widths, aspect ratios, or laser parameters for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061, and SS316; those values must come from later tables, figures, or supplementary information. The universal Keyhole number is defined using absorptivity η, laser power P, liquidus temperature Tl, substrate temperature T0, density ρ, heat capacity Cp, thermal diffusivity α, scan speed Vs, and laser radius r0: Ke = ηP/[(Tl−T0)√(πρCpαVs r0^3)]. The reported scaling law is e* = 0.4(Ke − 1.4), indicating an approximately linear relationship between aspect ratio and Keyhole number. The mode thresholds are conduction for Ke < 1.4 (e* = 0), transition for 1.4 ≤ Ke ≤ 6.0 (e* ≤ 2), and keyhole for Ke > 6.0 (e* > 2).

contexts.context: Allen et al. simultaneously used inline coherent imaging (ICI) to measure keyhole depth and integrating sphere radiometry (ISR) to measure absorptance, reported as coupling efficiency, during laser spot welding of AISI 316 stainless steel. The excerpt gives time-averaged absorptance/coupling-efficiency results but does not provide the corresponding absolute numerical keyhole-depth values. The onset thresholds for sustained keyhole formation were approximately 0.58 MW/cm² in argon and a lower threshold in air; the coupling efficiencies at those thresholds were 0.59 and 0.58, respectively. In conduction mode, argon produced a 50% ± 11% lower coupling efficiency than air, while in keyhole mode the argon value was only 8% ± 3% lower. The excerpt also states that depth and absorptance were acquired as time-resolved data and analyzed together, including oscillations during argon transition mode. contexts.context: Allen et al. simultaneously monitored melt-pool surface/keyhole depth with inline coherent imaging (ICI) and absolute laser absorptance with integrating sphere radiometry (ISR) while processing AISI 316 stainless steel (316L). ICI measured axial position at 200 kHz with 15 μm axial resolution and 0.6 μm single-point repeatability; positive depth denotes a keyhole and negative depth denotes a raised melt bead. ISR measured absolute absorptance with 4.4 μs temporal resolution. At 0.35 MW/cm² in conduction mode, absorptance plateaued near 0.21 in argon and rose to a maximum of 0.51 in air. In transition mode at 0.46 MW/cm², temporary keyholes in air produced absorptance up to 0.56, while depth showed sudden increases and fluctuations. In air at conduction conditions, the melt pool reached a maximum height of 83 μm; in argon, measurements occupied bands near −25 and 20 μm. At 0.58 MW/cm², sustained keyholes formed for the full 10 ms pulse in both gases, with lower growth and absorptance in argon. The excerpt reports threshold coupling efficiencies of 0.58 in air and 0.59 in argon. It does not provide the optical spot size or laser power, only irradiance values.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides qualitative descriptions of absorptance, keyhole formation, melt-pool geometry, and laser-processing conditions, but it does not report numerical absorptance values, keyhole depths, melt-pool dimensions, or specific laser parameters for individual metals. It explains that a stationary Gaussian laser produces the highest temperature beneath the beam center, causing vaporization, upward vapor ejection, and a vapor depression. As laser power or applied energy density increases, the depression can deepen through angle-dependent absorption and multiple internal reflections, producing conical or bimodal melt-pool shapes. At low applied energy density—defined here as power divided by scan velocity—the melt pool is small, shallow, and rounded; increasing energy density makes it deeper and larger. During scanning, the transverse pool remains nearly symmetric while the longitudinal pool develops a tail. The excerpt also states that absorption increases when light undergoes repeated irradiation of melt surfaces and depends on the local angle of incidence. No table or data concerning the flat-surface absorptivity of different metals at a wavelength of 1 μm appears in the supplied pages; that information would need to be obtained from another section, figure, table, or cited source in the full review.

contexts.question: Context: we are writing our own physics-based (first-principles, no parameters fitted to keyhole data) model of laser keyholing and keyhole-mode melt-pool size for laser powder bed fusion of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend, to replace the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module where conduction models (Eagar-Tsai) fail. Settings: 1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam with 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s, 30-150 C plate. The model has three parts: (1) absorptivity from the Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid metal with multiple reflections ray-traced inside the keyhole; (2) the keyhole's depth and shape from an energy balance at a wall held near the boiling point (moving line/point sources, Kaplan-style local conduction, evaporation losses, recoil pressure against surface tension); (3) the melt pool as the liquidus isotherm of the resulting sources. We will check it against Gan et al. 2021 (Nat. Commun. 12, 2379) X-ray keyhole depths for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061 and SS316, and against the AM Module's maps. Question: what direct measurements of laser absorptance during spot or line melting relate the absorbed fraction to the depression or keyhole depth, width or aspect ratio, for aluminium alloys (Al6061, AlSi10Mg, pure Al) and for comparison Ti-6Al-4V, 316L and IN625? Include integrating-sphere measurements made together with X-ray imaging (e.g. Simonds et al. 2021, Applied Materials Today), calorimetry (Trapp et al. 2017; Ye et al. 2019), and any keyhole-mode absorptance for Al at 1 um. Give the numbers: power, speed or dwell, spot size, measured absorptance, depression depth and width, and the reported relation (for example absorptance against depth/width), with DOIs, so that a ray-tracing absorptivity model can be checked against them. Also: what flat-surface absorptance at 1.06-1.07 um has been measured for liquid aluminium, and does a Drude model reproduce it?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a fitting-free inverse test: adjust absorptivity until a conduction model matches measured depth, then compare it with the physical ceiling. Depth increases monotonically with absorptivity, giving a unique inverse when possible; no solution or absorptivity above unity indicates keyhole necessity. contexts.question: Context: we are writing our own physics-based (first-principles, no parameters fitted to keyhole data) model of laser keyholing and keyhole-mode melt-pool size for laser powder bed fusion of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend, to replace the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module where conduction models (Eagar-Tsai) fail. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the specific Simonds et al. (2018) experimental values for stainless steel, including laser power, spot size, or measured absorptance ranges. It does, however, describe the expected absorptance evolution during keyhole formation. In conduction mode, a shiny molten surface produces approximately a single reflection. As a vapour depression develops and deepens into a keyhole, the number of internal reflections increases, raising absorptance through enhanced energy coupling. The excerpt cites ray-tracing results for 316L stainless steel in which increasing shallow-keyhole reflections from one to two raises absorptance by a factor of 1.3. Further reflections continue to increase absorption, but with diminishing returns, asymptotically approaching a maximum absorptance of 1. Because the keyhole geometry fluctuates, the number and paths of reflections also change, producing oscillations in time-resolved absorptance. These fluctuations are associated with keyhole instability and partial collapse, which can contribute to defects such as porosity and spatter.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that Ye et al.’s absorptivity relation is a closed-form, asymptotic exponential scaling with normalized enthalpy. The effective absorptivity increases toward a saturation value of 0.70, with decay constant 0.66; below the transition, fixed flat-surface values are used. The excerpt gives 0.34 for 316L and 0.27 for IN625, based on independent calorimetric values, but it does not provide a Ti-6Al-4V absorptance value. Normalized enthalpy is represented by β = AP/[ρ hs √(π a v σ³)], where hs is the heat content needed to reach melting, including latent heat. The absorptivity transition is indexed by normalized enthalpy. Keyhole classification is then based on aspect ratio rather than absorptivity alone: using depth divided by half-width, conduction corresponds to d/(w/2) < 1, transition to 1–2, and keyholing to >2. Thus, increasing normalized enthalpy changes the modeled absorptivity and identifies the transition, while the reported keyhole state is diagnosed through the resulting melt-pool depth-to-width ratio.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that aluminum alloys exposed to 1070 nm Yb-fibre lasers remained close to an absorptance of approximately 0.15 during the cited measurements. However, it does not provide separate values for Al6061, AlSi10Mg, Al1100, or Al5182, nor does it identify whether the quoted value corresponds specifically to laser spot melting or line melting. It also does not give numerical conduction-mode and keyhole-mode absorptance values for aluminum. Qualitatively, absorptance increases during heating before melting, then decreases once the molten surface becomes smoother. In conduction mode, a shiny melt pool produces comparatively fewer reflections and therefore lower coupling. When a vapour depression or keyhole forms, multiple reflections increase the energy coupling and absorptance; deeper keyholes produce more reflections and higher absorptance, asymptotically approaching a maximum of 1 in the limiting case. The excerpt gives a numerical example only for 316L stainless steel, where increasing shallow-keyhole reflections from one to two raised absorptance by a factor of 1.3, so that value should not be applied to aluminum.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report absorptance or coupling-efficiency measurements for Al6061, AlSi10Mg, Al1100, or Al5182, nor does it specify 1070 nm aluminum spot- or line-melting experiments. It instead discusses optical and calorimetric measurements for laser welding of molten stainless steel. In that experiment, coupling efficiency was approximately 30% at low incident energy, increased sharply after Ein = 2.9 J, nearly doubled by Ein = 3.8 J, and reached nearly 90% at the highest measured energy. The increase was interpreted as the transition from conduction-mode welding to keyhole welding, associated with enhanced absorptance from multiple reflections. Table 3 lists efficiencies ranging from approximately 0.25–0.31 at the lowest energies to 0.91 at the highest listed condition, with intermediate values including 0.35, 0.50, 0.55, 0.64, 0.70, 0.69, and 0.77. However, these values should not be treated as aluminum absorptance values or as conduction/keyhole values specifically for aluminum at 1070 nm.

Question: Context: we are writing our own physics-based (first-principles, no parameters fitted to keyhole data) model of laser keyholing and keyhole-mode melt-pool size for laser powder bed fusion of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend, to replace the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module where conduction models (Eagar-Tsai) fail. Settings: 1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam with 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s, 30-150 C plate. The model has three parts: (1) absorptivity from the Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid metal with multiple reflections ray-traced inside the keyhole; (2) the keyhole's depth and shape from an energy balance at a wall held near the boiling point (moving line/point sources, Kaplan-style local conduction, evaporation losses, recoil pressure against surface tension); (3) the melt pool as the liquidus isotherm of the resulting sources. We will check it against Gan et al. 2021 (Nat. Commun. 12, 2379) X-ray keyhole depths for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061 and SS316, and against the AM Module's maps. Question: what direct measurements of laser absorptance during spot or line melting relate the absorbed fraction to the depression or keyhole depth, width or aspect ratio, for aluminium alloys (Al6061, AlSi10Mg, pure Al) and for comparison Ti-6Al-4V, 316L and IN625? Include integrating-sphere measurements made together with X-ray imaging (e.g. Simonds et al. 2021, Applied Materials Today), calorimetry (Trapp et al. 2017; Ye et al. 2019), and any keyhole-mode absorptance for Al at 1 um. Give the numbers: power, speed or dwell, spot size, measured absorptance, depression depth and width, and the reported relation (for example absorptance against depth/width), with DOIs, so that a ray-tracing absorptivity model can be checked against them. Also: what flat-surface absorptance at 1.06-1.07 um has been measured for liquid aluminium, and does a Drude model reproduce it?

## Direct Measurements of Laser Absorptance During Keyhole Formation and Their Relation to Depression Geometry

### 1. Overview of the Measurement Landscape

Three complementary experimental techniques have directly measured absorptance during laser melting at 1070 nm under conditions relevant to laser powder bed fusion (LPBF):

**(a) Calorimetry** — Trapp et al. (2017) measured effective absorptivity of bare and powder-coated 316L, Al 1100, and W discs by direct calorimetric measurement of absorbed energy during single-track scanning at 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s, with a 1070 nm fibre laser focused to a 60 ± 5 µm (1/e²) diameter Gaussian spot over 30–540 W (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 1-2, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4, trapp2017insituabsorptivity media 513c2402). Post-process cross-sectioning provided track depth and width, but not time-resolved cavity geometry.

**(b) Integrating-sphere radiometry (ISR) combined with inline coherent imaging (ICI)** — Allen et al. (2020) simultaneously measured keyhole depth (ICI at 200 kHz, 15 µm axial resolution) and absolute absorptance (ISR, 4.4 µs resolution) during 10 ms stationary irradiation of AISI 316 stainless steel at 1070 nm through a 238 µm (1/e²) diameter spot, 100–410 W (allen2020simultaneousinoperando pages 2-4, allen2020simultaneousinoperando pages 1-2, allen2019monitoringlasermateriala pages 39-44).

**(c) Integrating-sphere radiometry combined with synchrotron X-ray imaging** — Simonds et al. (2020, 2021, 2024) coupled ISR with high-speed X-ray transmission imaging at the Advanced Photon Source. This enabled simultaneous measurement of absolute absorptance and two-dimensional projected cavity/melt-pool geometry with microsecond time resolution (simonds2020simultaneoushighspeedxray pages 2-3, simonds2021thecausalrelationship pages 6-7, simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 3-6).

### 2. Absorptance–Keyhole Depth Relationships

**Simonds et al. (2021)** provide the most explicit quantitative relationship between absorptance and keyhole depth. For Ti-6Al-4V at 201 W, 0.7 m/s, and a 49.5 µm spot, the normalized keyhole depth was found to be approximately linearly proportional to the absorptance-dependent normalized enthalpy β = AP/(πH_m D u a³)^(1/2), with Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.98 on a bare plate (slope 0.42) and r = 0.70 on a powder bed (slope 0.31) (simonds2021thecausalrelationship pages 7-8). The key physical mechanism is that a deeper, higher-aspect-ratio vapor depression produces more internal laser reflections, which increases absorptance, which in turn deepens the cavity further. When the keyhole aspect ratio decreases (e.g., during partial collapse at ~400 µs), absorptance falls rapidly (simonds2021thecausalrelationship pages 6-7, simonds2021thecausalrelationship pages 1-2).

**Simonds et al. (2020)** found that for Ti-6Al-4V during stationary irradiation at 113.6 W, initial absorptance was approximately 0.30, rising rapidly at ~0.45 ms when the process transitioned from conduction to keyhole mode. Among keyhole depth, width, and projected area, depth had the strongest correlation with absorptance (simonds2020simultaneoushighspeedxray pages 2-3).

**Allen et al. (2020)** reported that for 316 SS at a 238 µm spot, absorptance plateaued near 0.21 in argon conduction mode and reached 0.51 in air. At the keyhole threshold (0.58 MW/cm²), coupling efficiency reached 0.58–0.59, and absorptance exceeded 0.9 in deep keyhole mode (allen2020simultaneousinoperando pages 2-4, allen2023sheddinglightona pages 56-61). Absorptance and vapour-depression depth fluctuations occurred at similar kilohertz-scale frequencies and correlated with one another (allen2023sheddinglightona pages 56-61).

### 3. Calorimetric Absorptance Data (Trapp et al. 2017)

For **316L** (bare disc, 500 mm/s): absorptivity was 0.29–0.31 at low power, rose sharply at a keyhole-formation threshold of approximately 70 W, and saturated at approximately 0.78, corresponding to a keyhole depth of roughly 300 µm. At 1500 mm/s the keyhole transition shifted to higher power, and 540 W produced a keyhole only about 207 µm deep (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4). For powder layers (~100 µm thick), low-power absorptivity was about twice that of the bare disc, dropped sharply upon full powder consolidation/melting, then rose again upon keyholing (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 1-2).

For **Al 1100** (bare disc, 1500 mm/s): absorptivity was approximately 0.10 at low power, began its keyhole-driven rise near 200 W, and reached approximately 0.50–0.55 at 540 W (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6, trapp2017insituabsorptivity media 513c2402). Both Al and W exhibited lower absorptivity than 316L and required higher power to initiate keyholing (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7).

### 4. Aluminium-Specific Absorptance Data

Directly measured absorptance data for aluminium alloys at 1 µm with simultaneous keyhole geometry remain scarce relative to Ti-6Al-4V and 316L:

- **Trapp et al. (2017)**: Al 1100 bare, 1070 nm, 60 µm spot, 1500 mm/s — conduction-mode absorptivity ~0.10, rising to ~0.55 in keyhole mode at 540 W (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6, trapp2017insituabsorptivity media 513c2402).
- **Simonds et al. (2024), AM-Bench 2022**: Bare polished Al 5182 (NIST SRM 1241c), 1070 nm, 122.5 µm (1/e²) spot — stationary 501 W with 1.98 ms exposure. Keyhole onset (defined as absorptance ≥ 35%) occurred at approximately 0.189 ms, with a nearly threefold absorption increase within microseconds of cavity formation. In scanning mode (473 W, 0.7 m/s), maximum melt-pool depth was 88.8 ± 0.4 µm and width 326 ± 16 µm (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 3-6, simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 8-10). Aluminum keyhole formation was much less repeatable than Ti-6Al-4V, with ±190 µs spread for stationary and ±650 µs for scanning (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 8-10). The full time-resolved datasets are archived at NIST (DOI: 10.18434/mds2-2525) (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 1-3).
- **Reed (2024, thesis)**: Al alloys remain near an absorptance of approximately 0.15 at 1070 nm during heating before melting (reed2024timeresolvedabsorptancein pages 27-31, reed2024timeresolvedabsorptanceina pages 27-31).

No published study was found that simultaneously measured keyhole depth and absorptance for AlSi10Mg or Al6061 specifically. The Gan et al. (2021) X-ray dataset includes Al6061 keyhole depths but without concurrent absorptance measurement.

### 5. Keyhole Geometry Benchmarks Without Concurrent Absorptance (Gan et al. 2021)

Gan et al. (2021) measured operando keyhole depths by high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061, and SS316 at 100–520 W, 0.3–1.2 m/s, and spot sizes of 44–70 µm (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 2-3). They defined the dimensionless Keyhole number Ke = ηP / [(T_l − T_0) √(π ρ C_p α V_s r_0³)] and reported a universal linear scaling law for normalized keyhole aspect ratio: e* = e/r₀ = 0.4(Ke − 1.4), with conduction mode at Ke < 1.4, transition at 1.4 ≤ Ke ≤ 6.0 (e* ≤ 2), and keyhole mode at Ke > 6.0 (e* > 2) (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2). Aspect-ratio fluctuation scaled as Δe* = 0.36 Ke^0.86; small fluctuations below Ke ≈ 16 and chaotic keyholes above Ke ≈ 30 (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 2-3). The absorptivity η used in the Keyhole number was taken from literature rather than measured simultaneously.

### 6. Ye et al. (2019) Absorptance Scaling Law

Ye et al.'s absorptance model, as reported in secondary sources, provides a process-dependent effective absorptivity: A_e = 0.70 [1 − exp(−0.66 β A_m L_th*)], where β is the normalized enthalpy, A_m is the conduction-mode baseline absorptance, and L_th* = D/(2σ u) is the normalized thermal diffusion length. The saturation value is 0.70. The baseline absorptances used are A_m = 0.34 for 316L and 0.27 for IN625 (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5, weaver2022laserspotsize pages 6-8). The keyhole threshold corresponds to normalized depth d/(2σ) > 1 (weaver2022laserspotsize pages 6-8). This scaling was fitted to calorimetric data across multiple alloys and process conditions.

The key findings for liquid aluminium specifically are:

- **Krishnan & Nordine (1993)** measured optical properties and emissivities of electromagnetically levitated liquid metals including aluminium by ellipsometry/polarimetry over 360–990 nm and temperatures of 1200–1600 K. Their reported liquid Al normal spectral emissivity (equivalent to absorptance for an opaque equilibrium surface) was approximately 0.04, but this datum does not extend to 1064 nm and must be extrapolated (krishnan1993opticalpropertiesand pages 6-11, krishnan1993opticalpropertiesand pages 1-6). For comparison, liquid Cu showed emissivity 0.085 and liquid Ni 0.31 at 1064 nm (krishnan1990spectralemissivitiesand pages 21-24).

- **Schmid et al. (2012)** used a custom high-temperature rotating-compensator ellipsometer with a 1070 nm SLED source to measure n and k through the solid-liquid transition. They published results for Au and Ag but not for Al at 1070 nm. They noted that temperature-dependent Drude-model predictions can diverge substantially from experiment, particularly for liquid metals (schmid2012measuringopticalproperties pages 1-3).

- **Drude-model applicability**: For aluminium, the free-electron Drude model is physically plausible at wavelengths above approximately 1 µm, where aluminium follows nearly-free-electron behavior and interband transitions (prominent below ~0.8 µm) are negligible (schmid2012measuringopticalproperties pages 1-3). However, the available experimental evidence does not establish that an unadjusted room-temperature Drude model, extrapolated to liquid-phase temperatures, quantitatively reproduces the flat-surface absorptance of liquid Al at 1064–1070 nm. The Drude model qualitatively predicts the correct trend (small absorptance increasing with temperature) but may require temperature-dependent collision-frequency adjustments. For gold and silver at 1070 nm, Schmid et al. showed that a Drude+Lorentz combined model was needed for quantitative accuracy, particularly near and above the melting point (schmid2012measuringopticalproperties media 6b6d82cf).

- **Practical validation band**: Given the sparsity of direct measurements, a reasonable validation band for the Drude-predicted normal-incidence absorptance of liquid Al at 1064–1070 nm is approximately 0.05–0.15. The lower end corresponds to the extrapolated Krishnan value and clean-interface Drude prediction; the upper end includes the effect of oxide, finite surface roughness, and the higher calorimetric values measured by Trapp et al. for polished Al 1100 at low power (~0.10) (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6, krishnan1993opticalpropertiesand pages 6-11).

### 8. Summary and Recommendations for Model Validation

For a first-principles keyhole model of LPBF aluminium alloys at 1070 nm:

1. **Flat-surface Fresnel absorptance**: Use a Drude model for the dielectric function of liquid Al at 1070 nm, but validate against the Krishnan/Nordine emissivity data (~0.04 at shorter wavelengths), the Trapp et al. calorimetric low-power value (~0.10 for polished Al 1100), and the Simonds AM-Bench pre-keyhole absorptance. Expect the normal-incidence absorptance to fall in the range 0.05–0.15 for a clean flat liquid Al surface.

2. **Absorptance vs. keyhole depth**: The strongest quantitative benchmark is Simonds et al. (2021) for Ti-6Al-4V (r = 0.98 linear correlation between normalized depth and absorptance-based enthalpy) (simonds2021thecausalrelationship pages 7-8). For Al, the Simonds et al. (2024) AM-Bench dataset provides time-resolved absorptance paired with X-ray melt-pool images for Al 5182 (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 3-6, simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 1-3). The NIST archived data (DOI: 10.18434/mds2-2525) should be downloaded for detailed ray-tracing comparison.

3. **Keyhole depth validation**: Use the Gan et al. (2021) X-ray depths for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061, and SS316 at 100–520 W, 0.3–1.2 m/s, 44–70 µm spots (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 2-3, gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2). The Keyhole number Ke provides a universal framework relating absorptivity, process parameters, and keyhole aspect ratio.

4. **316L comparison**: Trapp et al. (2017) absorptivity vs. power curves (60 µm spot, 100–540 W, three speeds) provide the most comprehensive calorimetric dataset (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 1-2, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4, trapp2017insituabsorptivity media 513c2402). Allen et al. (2020) offer simultaneous depth–absorptance data for 316 SS at a larger 238 µm spot (allen2020simultaneousinoperando pages 2-4, allen2020simultaneousinoperando pages 1-2).

5. **Ye et al. scaling law**: The empirical absorptance model A_e = 0.70[1 − exp(−0.66 β A_m L_th*)] with A_m = 0.34 (316L) or 0.27 (IN625) provides a useful check on whether your ray-traced absorptance reproduces the correct functional dependence on normalized enthalpy (hong2026fittingfreediagnosisof pages 4-5, weaver2022laserspotsize pages 6-8).

No published simultaneous absorptance + keyhole-depth dataset was found specifically for AlSi10Mg or for a hypereutectic Al–24Si blend. The closest aluminium dataset is the Simonds et al. (2024) Al 5182 integrating-sphere + X-ray data at 501 W / 122.5 µm stationary and 473 W / 0.7 m/s scanned (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 3-6).

info.query: Context: we are writing our own physics-based (first-principles, no parameters fitted to keyhole data) model of laser keyholing and keyhole-mode melt-pool size for laser powder bed fusion of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend, to replace the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module where conduction models (Eagar-Tsai) fail. Settings: 1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam with 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s, 30-150 C plate. The model has three parts: (1) absorptivity from the Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid metal with multiple reflections ray-traced inside the keyhole; (2) the keyhole's depth and shape from an energy balance at a wall held near the boiling point (moving line/point sources, Kaplan-style local conduction, evaporation losses, recoil pressure against surface tension); (3) the melt pool as the liquidus isotherm of the resulting sources. We will check it against Gan et al. 2021 (Nat. Commun. 12, 2379) X-ray keyhole depths for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061 and SS316, and against the AM Module's maps. Question: what direct measurements of laser absorptance during spot or line melting relate the absorbed fraction to the depression or keyhole depth, width or aspect ratio, for aluminium alloys (Al6061, AlSi10Mg, pure Al) and for comparison Ti-6Al-4V, 316L and IN625? Include integrating-sphere measurements made together with X-ray imaging (e.g. Simonds et al. 2021, Applied Materials Today), calorimetry (Trapp et al. 2017; Ye et al. 2019), and any keyhole-mode absorptance for Al at 1 um. Give the numbers: power, speed or dwell, spot size, measured absorptance, depression depth and width, and the reported relation (for example absorptance against depth/width), with DOIs, so that a ray-tracing absorptivity model can be checked against them. Also: what flat-surface absorptance at 1.06-1.07 um has been measured for liquid aluminium, and does a Drude model reproduce it?
